title: Digital Entrepreneurship and Remote Work
subtitle: Choose the right online income model, work reliably with clients across time zones, get paid safely and launch a digital service with a 90-day plan.
description: A practical course for women who want to earn through remote jobs, freelancing, online selling or digital products from Nigeria. You will build a work-ready setup with backups, learn the written and tool habits remote clients expect, receive cross-border payments safely, and finish with a launched service and a measurable 90-day plan.
outcomes: Compare remote jobs, freelancing, e-commerce and digital products and choose a starting model that fits your skills and time
Run a reliable remote setup with a data budget, power and internet backups, and correct time-zone scheduling
Use shared Drive folders, version history, task boards and written updates to deliver work remotely
Calculate what you receive after payment fees and currency conversion, and avoid common remote-work scams
Apply precisely for remote roles and price a digital product using break-even sales
Launch a digital service with a 90-day activity plan and responsible handling of client data
audience: Women with a marketable skill and basic smartphone or computer confidence who want to earn reliably from clients and employers beyond their local area.
tools: Smartphone (a laptop helps for documents, spreadsheets and design work)
Earphones or headset with a microphone
Mobile data, ideally on two SIMs from different networks, and a power bank
A Google account (Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Calendar, Meet)
Free Trello account or a Google Sheet for task tracking

modules.title: Foundations: Choosing Your Digital Income Model and Getting Work-Ready
modules.overview: There is more than one way to earn online, and each one pays, grows and fails differently. This module helps you choose the model that fits your skills and life, then prepares your data, power, device and working hours so that clients in Lagos, London or New York can rely on you.

lessons.title: Four ways to earn online: remote job, freelancing, e-commerce and digital products
objectives: Describe the four main digital income models and how money flows in each
Compare the models on income stability, control, start-up cost and skills needed
Match your own skills and circumstances to one model to start with
Recognise income-model promises that are unrealistic

blocks.text: People say 'make money online' as if it were one thing. It is not. There are **four different models**, and the daily work, the way money arrives and the risks are very different in each. Choosing the right one for this season of your life saves you months of effort in the wrong direction.

blocks.name: work-from-anywhere
blocks.alt: A woman working on a laptop with a world map behind her
blocks.caption: Digital work lets your skill travel even when you stay at home, but each income model travels differently.

blocks.text: Model 1: the remote job

A **remote job** is employment where you work for one organisation from home. You have a manager, set duties, and a fixed monthly salary or a fixed contract fee. Examples include customer support agent, virtual assistant on a part-time contract, social media coordinator, data entry clerk or online tutor for a tutoring company. The big advantage is **predictable income**. The trade-off is less control: the employer sets your hours, your tasks and often your tools. Competition for remote roles is strong because applicants can come from many countries.
Model 2: freelancing

A **freelancer** sells a defined service to several clients, project by project or on a monthly retainer. A retainer is a fixed monthly fee for an agreed amount of ongoing work. A freelancer might write blog posts, design flyers, manage Instagram pages or transcribe audio. You choose your clients and prices, but income goes up and down, and you must find the work yourself. If you choose this model, the WODDI Institute course Freelancing Fundamentals goes deeper into packaging and pricing.
Model 3: e-commerce

**E-commerce** means selling physical goods online: shea butter, ankara bags, baked snacks, children's clothes. The selling happens on WhatsApp catalogues, Instagram, Facebook Marketplace, Jumia or your own simple website, but the product is real and must be stored, packed and delivered. You need money for stock, and your profit depends on cost price, delivery and returns. The internet widens your market; it does not remove the work of a shop.
Model 4: digital products

A **digital product** is something you make once and sell many times as a file or access: a budget spreadsheet template, a recipe e-book, a set of Canva templates for church programmes, a recorded short course. There is no stock and no delivery cost. The catch: sales usually start slowly, because people must first trust you and find you. Digital products work best for someone who already has an audience or teaching ability.

head: Model
How money arrives
Start-up cost
Main risk
rows: Salary or fixed contract fee, usually monthly
Uneven income; must keep finding clients
Per sale, minus product and delivery costs
Per download or access, many times
Low money, high time to create
Slow sales until people trust and find you

blocks.title: Stability versus control
items: Remote job: stable, less control
Retainer freelancing: stable, more control
Hourly gig work: unstable, less control
Products and projects: unstable, more control
blocks.caption: Most people move across this grid over time, often starting stable and gaining control as their reputation grows.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a starting model
blocks.context: Ngozi, for example, is a 38-year-old secondary school teacher in Enugu with two children. She has strong English, uses Google Docs well and can spare about 15 hours a week, mostly evenings and Saturdays.
steps: She lists her skills: clear writing, explaining things simply, organising documents.
She rules out e-commerce for now because she has no money for stock and no space to store it.
She rules out a full-time remote job because her teaching hours clash with a 9am to 5pm schedule.
She compares freelancing (editing and proofreading documents) with a digital product (a lesson-plan template pack).
She chooses freelancing first, because it can bring money within weeks, and writes the template pack idea down as a later second stream once she has teacher contacts who trust her.
blocks.result: Ngozi starts with one model that fits her hours and skills, and keeps a second model as a planned next step rather than trying all four at once.

blocks.title: Promises that should make you stop
blocks.text: Be careful with offers that promise large, fixed daily earnings for 'simple online tasks', ask you to pay a registration or 'activation' fee before you can work, or pay you to recruit other people. Real employers and real clients pay you; they do not charge you to start. Task and recruitment schemes of this kind have cost many Nigerians their savings.

Whichever model you pick, three things stay the same: you need a **skill someone will pay for**, a **reliable way to work online**, and **trust**, which you build through clear communication and keeping your promises. The rest of this course works on all three, with a focus on the standards that remote clients and employers expect.

takeaways: Remote jobs, freelancing, e-commerce and digital products are different businesses with different risks.
Remote jobs give stability; freelancing and products give more control but uneven income.
Start with one model that fits your hours, money and skills; plan a second one for later.
Anyone who asks you to pay to start earning is not offering real work.

activity.title: Pick your starting model
steps: Write down your three strongest skills and the hours you can honestly work each week.
Copy the comparison table and add a column titled 'Fits me?' with yes, no or later for each model.
Choose one starting model and write two sentences on why it suits you now.
Write one 'later' model and what would need to be true before you start it.
activity.evidence: A photo or screenshot of your completed table and your two-sentence choice.

lessons.title: Your work-ready setup: device, data, power and a backup plan
objectives: List the minimum device and software needs for your chosen digital work
Measure your own data use and build a monthly data budget
Plan backup power and a second internet route for deadline days
Set up simple file backup so work is never lost

blocks.text: A client abroad does not see NEPA, network outages or a dead phone battery. They only see that your work arrived late or your call dropped. In Nigeria, a **backup plan for power and internet** is part of being professional, not an extra. This lesson helps you build a setup you can trust on the days that matter.

blocks.name: working-at-home
blocks.alt: A woman working at a desk at home with a laptop
blocks.caption: A small, reliable home setup with backups is worth more than an expensive device that fails on deadline day.

blocks.text: Device: what you actually need

Match the device to the work. Many tasks can start on a good **smartphone**: customer support on WhatsApp, social media management, simple Canva designs, transcription with earphones. A **laptop** becomes necessary for long documents, spreadsheets, heavy design, coding or any job that needs two windows open at once. Before buying, check the job requirement. Many remote job adverts state the minimum, for example a laptop with a webcam and a headset.

items: **Headset or earphones with a microphone**: they cut background noise on calls far more than a better phone does.
**Free office tools**: Google Docs, Sheets and Drive work in a browser or as phone apps.
**Up-to-date software**: install updates, because they fix security holes.
**A screen lock and a separate work email** so personal and client matters stay apart.

blocks.text: Data: measure, then budget

Guessing your data use leads to running out in the middle of a client call. Instead, **measure it**. On Android, open Settings and look for Network or Data usage; on iPhone, open Settings then Mobile Data. Note how much each app used over one normal work week. Video calls and uploading large files use the most. Turning your camera off on calls, and downloading files on Wi-Fi when you can, both save data.

Also stop data leaks you do not need. Turn off automatic video play in social apps, set WhatsApp media to download on Wi-Fi only, and stop phone backups from running over mobile data. Treat work data as a **business cost**: write it in your records each month like rent or transport, because it comes out of what you earn.

blocks.title: Worked example: a monthly data budget
blocks.context: Amina, for example, does social media management for two small businesses from Kano. She checks her phone's data usage screen after one ordinary work week.
steps: Her phone shows that work apps used 3.2 GB that week: Instagram and Facebook 1.8 GB, Google Meet 0.9 GB, WhatsApp 0.3 GB, Google Drive 0.2 GB.
Four weeks of the same work: 3.2 GB x 4 = 12.8 GB.
She adds about 25% as a safety margin for extra calls and uploads: 12.8 GB x 1.25 = 16 GB.
She compares data plans from two networks and chooses a plan of at least 16 GB that suits her budget, writing the price down as approximate because plans change often.
She keeps a small top-up on her second SIM for emergencies.
blocks.result: Amina knows she needs about 16 GB a month for work and budgets for it as a business cost, instead of running out in week three.

blocks.text: Power and internet backups

items: **Charge everything the night before** important calls and deadlines: phone, laptop, power bank.
**Keep a power bank** big enough to charge your phone at least once. For laptops, know where you can work if light goes off, such as a hub, office or a friend's place with an inverter.
**Use two SIMs from different networks.** When one network is weak in your area, switch the hotspot to the other.
**Work offline when you can.** In Google Docs, turn on offline access so you can keep typing without internet; it will sync later.
**Tell clients early** if a known problem is coming, such as a planned outage or travel.

blocks.title: Deadline-day backup plan
items: Main internet fails
Switch to second SIM
Still down: work offline
Message client before deadline
Deliver once connected
blocks.caption: Each step has a fallback, and the client hears from you before the deadline, not after it.

blocks.text: Never lose work: simple backups

Save client work in a **cloud folder** such as Google Drive, not only on your phone. If your phone is stolen or your laptop breaks, the files are safe. Use clear names, for example 'ClientName_Instagram-plan_2026-03_v2', so you and the client can always tell which version is the latest. Keep one folder per client, with sub-folders such as 'Briefs', 'Drafts' and 'Final'. Once a month, check that your phone's photos and documents are also backing up, because a client voice note or screenshot you need as proof can be lost with the phone. Turn on **2-Step Verification** for the Google account that holds client files, so a stolen password alone cannot open them.

blocks.title: Electricity safety at home
blocks.text: Use a surge protector or stabiliser for laptops and chargers, because power often returns with a surge. Do not overload one extension socket, keep cables away from water and from where children walk, and switch off and unplug equipment during heavy lightning storms.

takeaways: Match your device to the work; a headset matters more than a new phone.
Measure your real data use for a week, multiply by four and add a margin.
Two SIMs on different networks, a power bank and offline mode are your backups.
Keep client files in a cloud folder protected with 2-Step Verification.

activity.title: Build your setup sheet
steps: Write the device, headset and apps you will use for your chosen work.
Check your phone's data usage screen after one week and write the work apps' totals.
Calculate your monthly data need with a 25% margin.
Write your three-step backup plan for power and internet.
Create a Google Drive folder named 'Client work' and turn on 2-Step Verification.
activity.evidence: A one-page setup sheet plus a screenshot of your data usage screen.

lessons.title: Working across time zones and setting your availability
objectives: Convert times between West Africa Time, UK time and US Eastern time, including seasonal changes
Find the overlap hours between you and a client abroad
Write clear availability and response-time statements
Plan a weekly work schedule that protects family time

blocks.text: When you work with clients outside Nigeria, time becomes a skill. A meeting at '3pm' means nothing until you know **whose 3pm**. Missing a call because of a time-zone mistake is one of the fastest ways to lose a new client, and it is completely avoidable.

blocks.name: online-calendar
blocks.alt: A person looking at an online calendar with scheduled events
blocks.caption: Putting every client meeting in a calendar with the correct time zone prevents most scheduling mistakes.

blocks.text: The time zones you will meet most

Nigeria uses **West Africa Time (WAT)**, which is **UTC+1** all year. UTC is the world's reference time. Nigeria does not change its clocks. Many client countries do. The **United Kingdom** uses GMT (UTC+0) in winter and British Summer Time (UTC+1) from late March to late October. The **US East Coast** (New York, Washington) uses UTC-5 in winter and UTC-4 from March to early November, when daylight saving time applies.

head: Client location
Their time vs Lagos in their summer
Their time vs Lagos in their winter

blocks.title: Let the calendar do the maths
blocks.text: In Google Calendar, check that your own time zone is set to Lagos (West Africa Time). When a client sends an invite, it will appear at the right local time. When you propose times, write both, for example '4pm WAT / 11am New York time', and double-check with a world clock app or a site such as timeanddate.com, especially in March, October and November when clocks change.
Finding the overlap

The **overlap** is the set of hours when both you and the client are normally working. Calls and quick questions should happen there. Everything else can be done **asynchronously**, which means you each work at different times and communicate in writing.

blocks.title: Worked example: overlap with a New York client in summer
blocks.context: Funke, for example, does virtual assistant work from Ibadan. A new client in New York works 9am to 5pm New York time and wants a short weekly call. It is July, so New York is 5 hours behind Lagos.
steps: Convert the client's day to WAT: 9am + 5 hours = 2pm WAT; 5pm + 5 hours = 10pm WAT.
Funke's own working window is 9am to 6pm WAT, because evenings are for her children's homework.
Overlap = the hours inside both windows: 2pm to 6pm WAT, which is 9am to 1pm New York time.
She proposes 'Tuesdays at 3pm WAT / 10am New York time' for the weekly call.
She notes that in November, when New York moves to winter time, the same 3pm WAT becomes 9am New York time, and she will confirm with the client before the change.
blocks.result: Funke offers a call time that fits both days and has already planned for the clock change, which shows the client she is careful and organised.

blocks.title: A Lagos day with a New York client
items: 9am WAT: focused solo work
2pm WAT: client day starts
3pm WAT: weekly call
6pm WAT: send end-of-day update
Evening: family, phone off
blocks.caption: Solo work happens in the morning, contact happens in the overlap, and a written update closes the day.

blocks.text: Write your availability down

Clients relax when they know exactly when they can reach you. Put a short **availability statement** in your proposals, email signature or WhatsApp Business profile. Promise a **response time** you can keep every day, not your best day. Twenty-four hours on working days is common and reasonable for freelancers; a remote employer may set its own rule.

items: 'Working hours: Monday to Friday, 9am to 6pm West Africa Time (UTC+1).'
'I reply to messages within one working day. For urgent issues during working hours, call or send a WhatsApp message marked URGENT.'
'I am not available on Sundays.'

blocks.title: Protecting your rest
blocks.text: Clients far away may message at your midnight. That does not mean you must reply at midnight. Turn on 'Do not disturb' for work apps after hours, and use WhatsApp Business away messages to tell people when you will reply. Steady, predictable replies build more trust than instant replies at every hour.
Plan the whole week, not only the calls

Time zones affect your week as well as your day. A client in the US may still be working on Friday evening in Lagos, and clients abroad have public holidays on different days from Nigeria's, so ask about theirs early. Block your week in a calendar: **focus blocks** for deep work at the hours you think best, **overlap blocks** for calls and quick replies, and **fixed family blocks** such as school runs and meals. Put deadlines in the calendar in the client's time zone and in yours, and plan to finish a day early. That spare day is what saves you when light or network fails.

takeaways: Nigeria is on WAT (UTC+1) all year; the UK and US change clocks, so the gap changes.
Find the overlap hours and keep calls inside them; work asynchronously the rest of the time.
Always write both time zones when proposing a meeting.
Publish working hours and a response time you can keep every single day.

activity.title: Your availability plan
steps: Choose one client location (London, New York or another) and write its time difference with Lagos in summer and winter.
Write your own working window in WAT and calculate the overlap with that client's 9am to 5pm day.
Write a three-line availability statement with hours, time zone and response time.
Set up an away message in WhatsApp Business or an email signature with your hours.
activity.evidence: Your written overlap calculation and a screenshot of your away message or signature.

quiz.q: Kemi has no savings for stock, can work 10 hours a week, and is a skilled proofreader. Which starting model fits her best right now?
options: Recruiting others into an online task scheme
quiz.explain: Freelancing uses the skill she already has, needs little money to start, and can fit into 10 flexible hours. E-commerce needs stock money, and a full-time job does not fit her hours.

quiz.q: Which statement about digital products is most accurate?
options: They sell well immediately because there is no stock
They need a warehouse and delivery riders
They always pay a fixed monthly salary
They are made once and sold many times, but sales often start slowly until people trust and find you
quiz.explain: Digital products have no stock or delivery cost, but buyers need to know and trust the seller, so early sales are usually slow.

quiz.q: Over one week, Bisi's work apps used 2.5 GB. Using the method from this module with a 20% margin, about how much data should she budget each month?
quiz.explain: 2.5 GB x 4 weeks = 10 GB. Adding 20% gives 10 x 1.2 = 12 GB.

quiz.q: It is August. A London client asks for a call at 2pm London time. What time is that in Lagos?
quiz.explain: In summer the UK uses British Summer Time (UTC+1), the same as WAT, so 2pm London is 2pm in Lagos.

quiz.q: Halima's internet fails two hours before a client deadline. According to the backup plan, what should she do first?
options: Switch her hotspot to her second SIM on another network
Wait until the network returns, then apologise
Tell the client the next day what happened
quiz.explain: The first fallback is the second SIM. If that fails she works offline and messages the client before the deadline, not after.

quiz.q: Which availability promise is the most professional for a new freelancer?
options: 'I reply instantly, any time, day or night'
No statement, so clients are not disappointed
'I reply within one working day; working hours are 9am to 6pm WAT, Monday to Friday'
quiz.explain: A clear, realistic response time and stated hours let clients plan, and you can keep the promise every day.

modules.title: Remote Delivery Standards: Tools, Communication and Getting Paid Safely
modules.overview: Remote clients judge you on what they can see: shared files, clear updates and work that arrives when promised. This module builds your remote toolkit, teaches the written communication habits of reliable remote workers, and shows how to receive money across borders without falling for scams.

lessons.title: The remote collaboration toolkit: shared files, task boards and video calls
objectives: Share Google Drive files with the correct permission level for each person
Use version history to recover or compare earlier work
Set up a simple task board with To do, Doing and Done lists
Run a short, well-prepared video call

blocks.text: In an office, a manager can walk to your desk and see what you are doing. In remote work, **your tools are your desk**. A client who can open one tidy shared folder, see a task board and join a call that starts on time will trust you quickly. You do not need expensive software. Free tools from Google and others are what many small teams use every day.

blocks.name: online-collaboration
blocks.alt: Two people working together on shared documents online
blocks.caption: Shared files and boards let a client see progress without asking you for it.

blocks.text: Shared files with Google Drive
When you share a file or folder in Google Drive, you choose a **role** for each person. Choosing the right role protects the work.

head: Role
What the person can do
Use it for
rows: Read and add comments or suggestions, but not change the text
Change, add and delete content, and by default share it further
Team members who must work in the file with you

blocks.text: Share with the client's **named email address** where you can, rather than 'anyone with the link', because a link can be forwarded. For drafts, give the client **Commenter** access so their changes come as suggestions you can accept, and the original stays safe. In Google Docs, **Suggesting** mode (the pencil icon at the top) shows proposed edits in colour, which is ideal for proofreading jobs.
Version history: your safety net

Google Docs, Sheets and Slides save automatically. Open **File, then Version history, then See version history** to see earlier versions, who changed what, and to restore an older one. You can also **name a version**, for example 'Sent to client 12 May', so you can always show exactly what you delivered. If a client says 'you deleted my paragraph', version history settles it calmly.
A task board everyone can see

A **task board** turns a project into cards you move from left to right. Trello is a popular free tool for this; a simple Google Sheet with the same columns also works. Each card is one task with a due date and, if needed, a checklist.

blocks.title: How a task moves on the board
items: Backlog: agreed tasks
To do this week
Doing
Waiting for client
Done
blocks.caption: Anyone who opens the board can see what is finished, what is in progress and what is waiting on the client.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting up a project workspace
blocks.context: Chioma, for example, has won a one-month job writing 8 blog posts for a small dental clinic in Lagos. The clinic manager, Mr Bayo, wants to review drafts.
steps: She creates a Drive folder 'Dental Clinic Blog 2026' with three sub-folders: Briefs, Drafts, Final.
She shares the main folder with Mr Bayo's email as Commenter, so he can suggest edits but cannot delete files.
She builds a Trello board with 8 cards, one per post, each with a due date: two posts a week.
She adds a 'Waiting for client' list so it is clear when a draft is with Mr Bayo, not with her.
When a post is approved, she moves the final copy into the Final folder, names the version 'Approved', and moves the card to Done.
blocks.result: Mr Bayo can see progress at any time without sending messages, and Chioma has a clear record of what was delivered and when.

blocks.text: Video calls that start well

items: Test the link, your microphone and your camera 10 minutes before. In Google Meet, the preview screen lets you check both.
Charge your device and close other apps that use data.
Sit facing a window or light, with a plain background. Use earphones to stop echo.
Send a short agenda before the call: three points and the decision you need.
Mute when you are not speaking, and keep to the time agreed.
After the call, send a written summary of decisions and next steps the same day.

blocks.title: Do not share more than you mean to
blocks.text: Before sharing your screen on a call, close personal chats, banking apps and other clients' files. Share one window instead of your whole screen where the app allows it. Never paste passwords into a shared document.

A simple rule ties this lesson together: **one home for every kind of information**. Files live in the shared folder, tasks live on the board, decisions live in writing. When a client asks 'where is it?', you should be able to answer with one link.
Use the client's tools when they have them

Larger clients and remote employers often already use their own tools, such as Slack for team chat, Microsoft Teams, Asana or Notion. Do not insist on yours. Ask in the first week: 'Which tools do you use for files, tasks and messages?' Most of these apps have free mobile versions and short help guides, and the skills carry over: a channel in Slack works like a WhatsApp group, a board in Asana works like Trello. Learn the basics in a day, set notifications for working hours only, and you will look like someone who has worked remotely for years.

takeaways: Give each person the smallest Drive role they need: Viewer, Commenter or Editor.
Version history lets you restore, compare and prove what you delivered.
A task board with a 'Waiting for client' list makes progress visible.
Test, prepare an agenda and send a written summary for every call.

activity.title: Build a sample client workspace
steps: Create a Drive folder for an imaginary or real client with Briefs, Drafts and Final sub-folders.
Write a one-paragraph draft in Google Docs, then name a version in Version history.
Share the folder with a friend as Commenter and ask them to add one suggestion.
Make a task board in Trello or Google Sheets with at least five cards and due dates.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of the folder sharing settings, the named version and the task board.

lessons.title: Writing like a reliable remote worker: briefs, updates and handling delays
objectives: Confirm a brief in writing before starting work
Write a clear status update using Done, Next and Blockers
Warn a client about a delay early and offer options
Deliver work with a handover note that prevents confusion

blocks.text: In remote work, **most of your professionalism is written**. Your client may never see you, but they read every message. Remote teams often work **asynchronously**: people work at different times and rely on clear written messages instead of quick chats. This lesson gives you four message types that cover most of a project: the brief confirmation, the status update, the delay warning and the handover note.

blocks.name: work-chat
blocks.alt: Two people exchanging work messages on screens
blocks.caption: Clear written messages replace the quick desk conversations remote teams cannot have.

blocks.text: 1. Confirm the brief before you start

A **brief** is the description of the job. Clients often explain it loosely in a voice note or call. Before you start, write it back in a short message and ask them to confirm. This one habit prevents most arguments later.

items: **What** you will deliver (for example, 12 Instagram post designs in Canva, square size).
**By when**, with the time zone.
**How many revisions** are included.
**What you need from them** and by when (logo, photos, approvals).
**Price and payment terms**, if not already in a written agreement.

blocks.text: 2. The status update: Done, Next, Blockers

A **blocker** is anything stopping you from moving forward, such as waiting for the client's photos. A short update on a fixed day, for example every Friday or at the end of each working day for a remote job, means the client never has to chase you.

blocks.title: A good status update
items: Done since last update
Next, with dates
Blockers and what you need
Any risk to the deadline
Link to the files
blocks.caption: Five short lines answer every question a remote manager usually has.

blocks.title: Worked example: a Friday update
blocks.context: Grace, for example, manages Facebook and Instagram for a fashion brand owner in Abuja who travels a lot. She sends this update every Friday by 5pm WAT.
steps: Done: 'Posted 5 of 5 planned posts this week. The Tuesday reel reached the most people so far.'
Next: 'Next week I will draft the 5 posts for the Sallah sale and send them to you on Tuesday for approval.'
Blockers: 'I need the new price list and 6 product photos by Monday, or the sale posts will be one day late.'
Risk: 'None if the photos arrive by Monday.'
Link: she pastes the link to the shared content calendar.
blocks.result: In under one minute of reading, the owner knows what happened, what is next, and exactly what Grace needs from her.

blocks.text: 3. Warning about a delay
Delays happen. What damages trust is **silence**. Tell the client as soon as you see the risk, not on the deadline day. Say what happened in one sentence, without long excuses, and offer choices.

blocks.title: A delay message that keeps the client
blocks.text: 'Hello Mrs Okafor, I want to warn you early: the power outage in my area since yesterday has slowed the video edit. I can either send the full video on Thursday instead of Wednesday, or send the first 60 seconds on Wednesday as planned and the rest on Thursday. Which do you prefer?'
4. The handover note

When you deliver, do not just send a file. A **handover note** lists what is included, where the files are, how to use them, and what happens next, such as the revision window. For example: 'Attached and in the Final folder: logo in PNG (for social media) and PDF (for printing). You have 2 rounds of revisions until 20 June. After that, changes are billed separately.'
Tone that works across cultures

Clients from different countries read tone differently. A safe style is **polite, short and specific**: a greeting, the main point first, one request per message, and a clear sign-off. Avoid long voice notes for clients abroad, because many cannot listen at work and they are hard to search later; send a written summary instead. Use the client's preferred name and title, and avoid slang or pidgin unless the client uses it first.

Keep important agreements **in writing on a channel you both use for work**, usually email for international clients. If something is agreed on a call or WhatsApp, follow up with a short email: 'As agreed on our call today...'. This becomes your record if there is ever a dispute about scope or payment.
Acknowledge every message, even before you have the answer

Remote clients worry most when a message seems to vanish. If you cannot answer fully, send a short **acknowledgement** within your stated response time: 'Received, thank you. I will check the figures and reply by 3pm WAT tomorrow.' Then keep that second promise. When a client sends several requests in one long message, reply with a numbered list that answers each point, so nothing is missed. Before sending any important message, read it once as if you were the client: is the main point in the first two lines, and is it clear what you need from them?

takeaways: Write the brief back to the client and get confirmation before you start.
Send regular updates with Done, Next and Blockers so no one has to chase you.
Warn about delays early, briefly, and with options.
Deliver with a handover note and keep agreements in writing.

activity.title: Write your four core messages
steps: Write a brief confirmation for a sample job using the five points in this lesson.
Write a status update using Done, Next, Blockers, Risk and Link.
Write a delay warning that offers the client two options.
Write a handover note for the same job, including the revision window.
Save all four as templates in Google Docs or your phone's notes.
activity.evidence: Your saved document with the four message templates.

lessons.title: Getting paid across borders and protecting your money and accounts
objectives: Compare common ways for Nigerian remote workers to receive local and foreign payments
Calculate what you actually receive after fees and currency conversion
Recognise the most common payment and fake-job scams
Secure your work accounts with strong passwords and 2-step verification

blocks.text: Earning the money is only half the job. You also need to **receive it safely, in a form you can use**, and keep your accounts from being taken over. Payment options change often in Nigeria, so this lesson teaches you how to compare them and what questions to ask, rather than promising that any one service will always be best.

blocks.name: online-payments
blocks.alt: A person receiving a payment on a phone
blocks.caption: Choose a payment route you can verify and withdraw from, before you start the work.

blocks.text: The main ways to receive payment

head: Route
Typical use
Things to check
rows: Local bank transfer or fintech account (for example Moniepoint, Opay, Kuda)
Account name matches the invoice; confirm the money is in your balance, not just a screenshot
Payment link or invoice (for example Paystack)
Nigerian and some foreign clients paying by card
Fees per transaction; when the money settles to your bank
Freelance marketplace (for example Upwork or Fiverr)
Clients you met on that platform
Platform service fees; withdrawal methods available in Nigeria; never move payment off the platform
Foreign clients and marketplaces paying in dollars, pounds or euros
Fees to receive and to withdraw; exchange rate used; identity verification
Domiciliary account at a Nigerian bank
Larger foreign-currency payments by bank transfer
Bank charges, documents needed, how long transfers take

blocks.text: Before you accept any foreign client, check three things on the provider's **official website or app**: the current fees, whether the service works for Nigerian users right now, and how you withdraw to your local account. Ask in trusted freelancer communities what is working this month, but always confirm on the official site.
Know what you will actually receive
The price you quote is not the money that lands. Fees and exchange rates take a share. Always calculate your **net amount** before you agree a price.

blocks.title: Worked example: from invoice to naira
blocks.context: Zainab, for example, agrees a $300 project with a client in Canada, paid through a receiving service. The figures below are for practice only; she checks the real fees and rate on the day.
steps: Invoice amount: $300.
Suppose the service charges a 1% receiving fee: $300 x 0.01 = $3, leaving $297.
Suppose she withdraws to her naira account at a rate of ₦1,450 per $1 and a 2% conversion margin is built into that rate. She receives $297 x ₦1,450 = ₦430,650.
She compares this with the open-market rate shown that day, for example ₦1,480: $297 x ₦1,480 = ₦439,560. The difference, ₦8,910, is the hidden cost of conversion.
Her real take-home is ₦430,650, which is about 97% of the full $300 at the higher rate.
blocks.result: Zainab now quotes knowing roughly 3% will go on fees and conversion, and she includes this in her price instead of being surprised.

blocks.text: Scams that target remote workers

blocks.title: Real client or scam?
items: Real client
Likely scam
left: Uses official company email or platform
Happy to sign a simple agreement
right: Asks you to pay a fee first
Moves you off the platform quickly
blocks.caption: If any item on the right appears, stop and verify before you send money, documents or codes.

items: **Pay-to-work:** 'training fees', 'starter kits' or 'account activation' before you earn. Real employers do not charge you to be hired.

**Overpayment:** a 'client' sends more than agreed, often by a cheque or a transfer that is later reversed, and asks you to refund the difference. Wait until the money is cleared and confirmed by your bank, and refund only to the original source.
**Fake screenshot:** a payment 'receipt' image with no money in your account. Only trust your own bank or app balance.
**Off-platform pressure:** a marketplace client who wants to pay outside the platform. You lose the platform's payment protection, and it usually breaks the platform's rules.
**Task scams:** being paid small amounts to like videos or rate products, then asked to deposit money to 'unlock' bigger earnings.

blocks.title: Protect your accounts
blocks.text: Use a different strong password for your email, bank and work platforms, ideally a passphrase of four or more random words, kept in a password manager. Turn on 2-Step Verification on Google and on your freelance platforms, and set a WhatsApp two-step verification PIN. Never share a one-time code (OTP) with anyone, even someone who says they are from your bank or the platform's support team.

Finally, keep a simple **income record**: date, client, amount invoiced, fees, amount received in naira. It shows your true earnings, helps you price better and gives you evidence if a payment goes missing.

For new clients, protect yourself with **deposits and milestones**. Ask for part of the fee before you start, for example 50%, and the rest on delivery. For longer projects, split the work into stages and get paid for each stage before starting the next. On marketplaces, work only on contracts the platform has funded. If a client refuses any deposit on a first job, keep the first stage small so your risk is small too.

takeaways: Check fees, availability in Nigeria and withdrawal method on the official site before you start a job.
Calculate your net amount after fees and conversion and include those costs in your price.
Never pay to get work, never refund an 'overpayment' before money clears, never trust a screenshot.
Strong unique passwords, 2-Step Verification and never sharing OTPs protect your income.

activity.title: Your payment and security plan
steps: Choose the payment route(s) for your first clients and write the fees from the official site, with today's date.
Calculate the net naira you would receive on a sample invoice of $100 or ₦50,000.
Turn on 2-Step Verification on your work email and set a WhatsApp two-step PIN.
Start an income record sheet with the columns from this lesson.
activity.evidence: Your fee notes and calculation, screenshots showing 2-Step Verification is on (hide codes), and the empty income sheet.

quiz.q: Amaka wants a client to review her draft and suggest changes without being able to delete anything. Which Google Drive role should she give?
quiz.explain: Commenter lets the client read and suggest or comment, but not change or delete the content.

quiz.q: A client claims Tola removed a section from a shared Google Doc. What is the calmest way to check?
options: Ask the client to resend the document
Open File, Version history to see who changed what and restore if needed
Delete the document and start again
quiz.explain: Version history shows every saved version and who made changes, and lets you restore an earlier version.

quiz.q: Which update best follows the Done, Next, Blockers format?
options: 'Finished 3 of 4 designs; final design due Thursday; I need your logo file by Tuesday.'
'Working hard on it, will update soon.'
quiz.explain: It states what is done, what comes next with a date, and the exact blocker the client must solve.

quiz.q: Ese realises on Monday that a Wednesday deadline is at risk. What should she do?
options: Say nothing and hope to finish
Ask a friend to finish it secretly
Message the client now, explain briefly and offer two options
quiz.explain: Early warning with options keeps trust; silence until the deadline damages it.

quiz.q: A new 'client' sends ₦150,000 for a ₦50,000 job and asks Rukky to transfer back ₦100,000 quickly. What should she do?
options: Confirm in her own bank app that the money has cleared, and refund only to the original source if it is real
Refund to a different account the client names
quiz.explain: This is the overpayment pattern. Transfers and cheques can be reversed. Confirm cleared funds yourself and never refund to a new account.

quiz.q: Using the same method as the lesson, an invoice of $200 has a 1% fee and is converted at ₦1,400 per $1. How much naira arrives?

modules.title: Growing Your Digital Enterprise: Remote Roles, Products and Community Impact
modules.overview: With your setup and standards in place, this module helps you grow: applying well for remote roles, adding a digital product or online shop as a second income stream, and launching your digital service with a 90-day plan that can also open doors for other women.

lessons.title: Finding and winning remote jobs and contract roles
objectives: Search for genuine remote roles using filters and reputable job boards
Tailor a CV and short cover note to a specific remote role
Prepare for a video interview and a paid or unpaid test task
Spot the warning signs of fake remote job offers

blocks.text: A remote job or longer contract gives the steady income that freelancing often lacks. Many Nigerian women now work as remote customer support agents, virtual assistants, content moderators, online tutors and project coordinators. The competition is real, so the women who succeed are usually not the most talented applicants. They are the ones who **apply precisely** and **show remote-work habits** from the first message.

blocks.name: job-hunt
blocks.alt: A woman searching job listings on a large screen
blocks.caption: A focused search with the right filters beats sending the same CV to hundreds of adverts.

blocks.text: Where to look

items: **LinkedIn Jobs:** search your role, then set the location type filter to 'Remote'. Read whether the role accepts applicants from Nigeria or only from certain countries; many adverts say this near the bottom.
**Remote-focused job boards** such as We Work Remotely and Remote OK, which list roles from companies that hire remotely.
**Company careers pages:** if you like a company, check its own website. Applying there avoids fake copies of the advert.
**Nigerian and African networks:** professional groups, alumni groups and women's networks often share remote roles from trusted members.

blocks.title: Read the location line
blocks.text: 'Remote' does not always mean 'anywhere'. Some roles are 'Remote, US only' or 'Remote within Europe' because of tax and employment law. Applying to those wastes your time. Look for 'Remote (Worldwide)', 'Remote, Africa' or a time zone range such as 'UTC-1 to UTC+3', which includes Nigeria.
Tailor your CV for remote work

Many companies use an **applicant tracking system (ATS)**, software that scans CVs for the skills listed in the advert. Use the advert's own words for skills you genuinely have, keep the layout simple (no tables or text inside pictures), and save it as a PDF unless told otherwise. Add a short line that proves remote readiness.

blocks.title: Worked example: tailoring one CV to one advert
blocks.context: Joy, for example, from Port Harcourt, finds a remote 'Customer Support Associate' role open to applicants in Africa. The advert asks for written English, experience with Zendesk or similar tools, and availability 2pm to 10pm WAT.
steps: She highlights the advert's key words: written communication, ticketing system, customer satisfaction, evening shift.
She rewrites her retail job line from 'Attended to customers' to 'Resolved about 40 customer enquiries a day in person and on WhatsApp, keeping a written log of every complaint'.
She adds the free Freshdesk tutorial she completed under Skills, describing it honestly as 'self-taught, practice account'.
She adds a 'Remote setup' line: 'Laptop, headset, two internet providers, power backup; available 2pm to 10pm WAT.'
She writes a 5-sentence cover note that names the company, the role and one specific reason she fits, and she checks every sentence for spelling.
blocks.result: Joy sends one carefully matched application instead of twenty generic ones, and her CV now answers the employer's main remote questions before they ask.

blocks.title: What gets you hired remotely
items: Proof of results
Clear written English
Remote setup and availability
Matching skills from the advert
blocks.caption: Matching skills gets you past the scan; setup, writing and real results win the interview.

blocks.text: Interviews and test tasks

Remote interviews happen on video. Use the call checklist from Module 2, and prepare short stories using **STAR**: the Situation, the Task, the Action you took and the Result. Expect remote-specific questions: 'How do you manage your time without supervision?', 'Tell us about a problem with your internet and how you handled it', 'How do you keep a manager updated?'. Your answers from this course, such as your backup plan and update routine, are exactly what they want to hear.

Many employers set a **test task**, such as answering three sample customer emails. A short test is normal. A long task that looks like real work for their business, such as writing ten full articles, is not; ask whether it is paid, or offer a shorter sample. Never send original files you have not been paid for without a watermark or a limited preview.

Keep a simple **application tracker**: company, role, link, date applied, contact person, stage and next action. Follow up once, politely, about a week after the closing date if you have heard nothing. Rejections are normal in remote hiring, even for strong candidates, so judge yourself by the quality of each application and keep going. After every interview, write down the questions you were asked; your answers get sharper each time.

blocks.title: Signs of a fake remote job
blocks.text: Be very careful if the 'interview' happens only by text chat on Telegram or WhatsApp, if you are offered the job without any real interview, if they send you a cheque to buy equipment from 'their supplier', or if they ask for your BVN, bank login or OTP. Check that the recruiter's email uses the company's own domain and that the job also appears on the company's real website.

takeaways: Use the Remote filter and remote job boards, and read which countries a role accepts.
Mirror the advert's skill words honestly and add a remote setup line to your CV.
Prepare STAR stories about working without supervision and handling outages.
Text-only interviews, equipment cheques and requests for BVN or OTP signal a fake job.

activity.title: One precise application
steps: Find three genuine remote adverts open to applicants in Nigeria or Africa and save the links.
Choose one and list its key skill words.
Update your CV with matching (true) skills and a remote setup line.
Write a 5-sentence cover note for that role.
Write two STAR stories that answer remote-work interview questions.
activity.evidence: The three saved links, your tailored CV as a PDF, your cover note and your two STAR stories.

lessons.title: Adding a second stream: digital products and selling online
objectives: Choose a digital product idea that grows from your existing service
Calculate the price and break-even number of sales for a digital product
Calculate profit per order for a physical product sold online
Respect copyright and licence rules when creating products

blocks.text: Once your first income model is working, a **second stream** protects you when clients are quiet. The best second stream grows from what you already do. A bookkeeper can sell a spreadsheet template; a caterer who already sells online can sell a recipe e-book; a social media manager can sell a 30-day content planner. This lesson covers both digital products and selling physical goods online, with the numbers that tell you whether each idea is worth it.

blocks.name: online-shopping
blocks.alt: A person browsing and buying products in an online shop
blocks.caption: An online shop or product page can earn while you sleep, but only if the numbers work.

blocks.text: Digital products that suit service providers

head: Your service
Possible product
Format
rows: Monthly cash book and budget template
Google Sheets or Excel file with instructions
Editable flyer templates for churches or events
Canva template link or design files
WAEC or Common Entrance practice packs
Small chops costing guide and recipes
PDF e-book with a costing sheet

blocks.text: You can sell from a WhatsApp catalogue with a payment link, or use a platform built for digital products, such as Selar, which was started in Nigeria, or Gumroad. These platforms deliver the file automatically after payment. Compare their fees and payout options on their official sites before choosing.

A good digital product page answers four questions in plain words: **who it is for**, **what problem it solves**, **exactly what the buyer gets** (number of pages, file type, whether it works on a phone), and **how to use it** after download. Add two or three clear screenshots, and a short video if you can. Include simple instructions inside the file too, because a buyer who cannot open or use the product will ask for a refund or never buy again. Decide your refund rule before launch and state it on the page.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a template and finding break-even
blocks.context: Ruth, for example, is a bookkeeper in Abeokuta. She wants to sell a 'Small Shop Cash Book' Google Sheets template to market women and small shop owners.
steps: Her costs to create it: about 20 hours of her time, which she values at ₦2,500 an hour (20 x ₦2,500 = ₦50,000), plus about ₦15,000 for a short promotion. Total cost: ₦65,000.
She checks similar templates and sets her price at ₦4,000 (approximate, market-tested).
Suppose the selling platform keeps about 10% per sale: ₦4,000 x 0.10 = ₦400, so she keeps ₦3,600.
Break-even sales = total cost ÷ amount kept per sale = ₦65,000 ÷ ₦3,600 = 18.06, so 19 sales.
Every sale after the 19th is profit, with no extra cost of stock.
blocks.result: Ruth knows she must sell 19 copies to recover her time and promotion money, and she can now set a realistic goal, such as 30 sales in three months through her existing clients and WhatsApp status.

blocks.title: Service feeds product, product feeds service
items: Do client work
Notice repeated questions
Package answer as product
Buyers discover your service
More client work
blocks.caption: Products built from real client problems sell better, and buyers often become service clients.

blocks.text: Selling physical goods online: count every naira
For physical products, profit per order must cover the item, packaging, payment fees and any delivery cost you absorb. Many online sellers lose money because they forget packaging or free delivery.

items: Add up the cost of one item: materials or buying price, plus packaging and label. For example, a jar of whipped shea butter: ₦1,800 ingredients + ₦600 jar and label = ₦2,400.
Add any cost you pay per order, such as a payment fee of about ₦100 and ₦300 towards delivery: ₦2,400 + ₦400 = ₦2,800.
Subtract from the selling price. At ₦4,500: ₦4,500 - ₦2,800 = ₦1,700 profit per jar.
Check the margin: ₦1,700 ÷ ₦4,500 = about 38%. If a promotion cuts the price to ₦3,500, profit falls to ₦700, so plan discounts carefully.

blocks.title: Copyright and licences
blocks.text: Only sell what you have the right to sell. Do not copy other people's e-books, photos, recipes written word-for-word, past exam papers that belong to an exam body, or brand logos. If you build templates with Canva or stock photos, read the platform's licence: some elements may be used in your own designs but not resold as stand-alone templates. Food and cosmetic products may also need NAFDAC registration before wider sale.

Start small: one product, one clear buyer, one channel. Test it with ten people you already know, ask what confused them, improve it, then promote it. A product that ten buyers recommend is a better foundation than ten products no one has tested.

takeaways: Build your second stream from problems you already solve for clients.
Break-even sales = total creation cost ÷ amount you keep per sale.
For physical goods, include packaging, payment fees and delivery in cost per order.
Sell only content you created or have a licence to resell.

activity.title: Test a second-stream idea
steps: List three questions clients or customers ask you often.
Turn one into a product idea and name its buyer and format.
Estimate creation hours and promotion cost, choose a price, and calculate break-even sales.
Ask five possible buyers if they would pay that price and write their answers.
activity.evidence: Your product idea sheet with the break-even calculation and the five buyer answers.

lessons.title: Launching your digital service, a 90-day plan and lifting other women
objectives: Assemble a launch kit: offer, work sample, availability and payment route
Set a 90-day plan with weekly activity targets and checkpoints
Handle client and team data in line with Nigeria's data protection law
Plan one way to share skills or work with other women

blocks.text: This final lesson brings everything together into a **launch**: the day you start actively offering your digital service, with a plan for the next 90 days. Your capstone project for this course is built from the work you do here, so keep everything you create.

blocks.name: launch-day
blocks.alt: A rocket launching to show the start of a new venture
blocks.caption: Launch day is the start of steady weekly action, not a single big announcement.

blocks.text: Your launch kit

items: **Offer line:** who you help, with what, and the result. For example: 'I manage Instagram pages for Abuja bakeries so they post 4 times a week without stress.'
**Work sample or portfolio:** 2 to 3 pieces, real or clearly labelled as practice samples.
**Availability statement** with time zone and response time (Module 1).
**Workspace templates:** shared folder, task board and your four message templates (Module 2).
**Payment route** checked on the official site, and your income record sheet (Module 2).
**Outreach list** of at least 20 named, suitable businesses or adverts.

blocks.text: The 90-day plan: activity you control

You cannot control whether a client says yes. You can control **how many good-quality approaches you make** and how well you follow up. Set targets for activity, then check results every 30 days and adjust.

Turn the 90-day target into a **weekly routine** you can keep alongside home duties. For example: Monday, research 5 new prospects; Tuesday and Wednesday, send 10 personal approaches; Thursday, follow up on last week's messages; Friday, update your tracker and portfolio. Ten approaches a week is about 40 a month. Protect paid client work first: if a busy week of delivery leaves no time for outreach, note it and catch up the next week rather than abandoning the plan. Write your three main measures at the top of your tracking sheet: approaches sent, replies, paid jobs.

blocks.title: Your first 90 days
items: Days 1-30: launch, 40 approaches
Day 30: review, adjust offer
Days 31-60: 40 approaches, deliver well
Day 60: ask for testimonials
Days 61-90: repeat clients, raise rates
blocks.caption: Each 30-day block ends with a review so the next block uses what you learned.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading 30-day results
blocks.context: Blessing, for example, offers CV writing and LinkedIn profile setup from Jos. In her first 30 days she tracked everything in a simple sheet.
steps: She sent 40 personal approaches: 25 on LinkedIn, 15 through WhatsApp contacts.
She got 8 replies: 8 ÷ 40 = 20% reply rate.
3 of the 8 became paid jobs: 3 ÷ 8 = 37.5% of replies converted, or 3 ÷ 40 = 7.5% of all approaches.
All 3 paying clients came from WhatsApp contacts; LinkedIn brought 5 replies but no sales yet.
Decision for days 31 to 60: keep 40 approaches, but send 25 through referrals and WhatsApp, rewrite her LinkedIn message to include a before-and-after sample, and ask each client for a referral.
blocks.result: Instead of feeling that 'LinkedIn does not work', Blessing has numbers that show where her clients come from and one specific thing to change.

blocks.text: Handle personal data responsibly

Remote work often means handling other people's personal data: customer lists, CVs, phone numbers, ID cards. Nigeria's **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), sets rules for how personal data is collected and used. For a small digital business, good practice includes:

items: Collect only the data you need for the job, and say what you will use it for.
Keep client files in your protected cloud folder, not in open WhatsApp groups.
Never reuse one client's customer list for another client or for your own marketing.
Delete or return personal data when the job ends, unless the client agrees otherwise.
Tell the client at once if their data may have been exposed, for example if your phone is stolen.

blocks.text: Lifting other women

Digital work can grow beyond one person. As you gain clients, you may need help with overflow work, and other women need a first opportunity. You can train one woman in your skill, refer clients you cannot take, or form a small team where one person handles design and another handles writing. If you subcontract, agree the task, deadline, quality standard and pay in writing, pay promptly, and remain responsible to your client for the final quality. Check each piece before it goes to the client, and do not share the client's private information with a helper unless the client has agreed. Some women in the WODDI network may also be ready to form a small digital cooperative or study group: meeting online once a week to share leads, review each other's portfolios and practise interviews costs little and keeps everyone moving.

blocks.title: Share honestly
blocks.text: When you share your story with other women, include the real numbers and the slow weeks, not only the wins. An honest account of '40 messages, 3 clients' helps a beginner far more than a screenshot of one big payment.

takeaways: A launch kit has six parts: offer, samples, availability, templates, payment route and outreach list.
Plan activity targets you control and review real numbers every 30 days.
Collect only needed personal data, store it securely and never reuse it across clients.
Train, refer or team up with other women, with clear written terms.

activity.title: Assemble your launch kit and plan
steps: Write your offer line and gather 2 to 3 work samples.
Build an outreach list of 20 named businesses or adverts.
Write your 90-day plan with targets for each 30-day block.
Set up a tracking sheet with columns: date, contact, channel, reply, outcome.
Write one sentence on how you will share your skill or work with another woman.
activity.evidence: Your launch kit folder link or screenshots, your 90-day plan and the tracking sheet.

quiz.q: A remote advert says 'Remote, US residents only'. Ifeoma lives in Ibadan. What should she do?
options: Skip it and look for roles open to Nigeria, Africa or a time zone range that includes UTC+1
Apply anyway with a US address
Apply twice to improve her chances
quiz.explain: Location limits usually exist for legal and tax reasons. Applying wastes time, and giving a false address is dishonest.

quiz.q: A 'recruiter' offers Dami a remote job after a Telegram text chat and then asks for her BVN and an OTP to 'set up payroll'. What is this most likely to be?
options: A fake job aiming to take over her accounts
quiz.explain: Text-only interviews and requests for BVN and OTP are classic signs of a fake job. Real employers never need your OTP.

quiz.q: A template costs ₦48,000 to create and promote. Each sale leaves the seller ₦3,000 after fees. How many sales are needed to break even?
A jar sells for ₦5,000. Item and packaging cost ₦2,700, and the seller pays ₦300 per order for fees and delivery. What is the profit per jar?
After 30 days, Ada sent 50 approaches and won 4 clients, all from referrals. What is the best next step?
options: Keep the activity level and shift more approaches toward referrals, while improving the weaker channel
Stop outreach because the rate is low
Change to a completely different service
quiz.explain: The numbers show where clients come from. Adjusting the channel mix based on evidence is the purpose of the 30-day review.

quiz.q: Which practice follows good data protection for a freelancer?
options: Using one client's customer list to market your own service
Storing client CVs in an open WhatsApp group
Keeping all client data forever just in case
Collecting only needed data, keeping it in a protected folder and deleting it when the job ends
quiz.explain: Collect the minimum, store it securely and delete or return it after the job, in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.

finalQuiz.q: Which digital income model usually gives the most predictable monthly income but the least control over hours?
finalQuiz.explain: A remote job pays a salary or fixed fee, but the employer sets hours and tasks.

finalQuiz.q: Someone offers 'easy online tasks' paying daily, but you must first pay ₦20,000 to activate your account. What is the right response?
options: Pay, because the earnings will cover it
Refuse: real work does not charge you to start
Recruit friends to share the fee
finalQuiz.explain: Paying to start earning is the signature of task and recruitment scams.

finalQuiz.q: Over one week, work apps used 4 GB of Uche's data. With a 25% safety margin, about how much should she budget per month?
In January, a New York client wants a call at 10am New York time. What time is that in Lagos?
finalQuiz.explain: In winter New York is on UTC-5, six hours behind Lagos (UTC+1). 10am + 6 hours = 4pm WAT.

finalQuiz.q: A client works 9am to 5pm London time in summer and you work 8am to 4pm WAT. What are the overlap hours in WAT?
finalQuiz.explain: In summer London equals WAT, so the client works 9am to 5pm WAT. Overlap with 8am to 4pm is 9am to 4pm.

finalQuiz.q: Which Drive setting best protects a final report you send a client to read?
options: Viewer, shared with the client's email
Editor, shared with the client's email
finalQuiz.explain: Viewer shared to a named email lets the client read without changing it, and limits who can open it.

finalQuiz.q: On a task board, why add a 'Waiting for client' list?
options: To make it clear when progress depends on the client, not on you
finalQuiz.explain: It shows blockers openly, so delays caused by missing client input are visible to everyone.

finalQuiz.q: Which message is the best handover note?
options: 'Let me know if you like it, I can change everything.'
'Final logo in PNG and PDF is in the Final folder; 2 revision rounds are included until 20 June.'
finalQuiz.explain: A handover note says what is delivered, where it is, and what happens next, such as the revision window.

finalQuiz.q: An invoice of $500 has a 1% receiving fee and is converted at ₦1,500 per $1. What arrives in naira?
Which CV change best helps a remote customer support application pass an applicant tracking system?
options: Putting all text inside a designed image
Listing every job since primary school
Using the advert's own skill words for skills she truly has, in a simple layout
Adding skills she does not have
finalQuiz.explain: ATS software scans text for the advert's skills; a simple layout and honest matching words help it read your CV.

finalQuiz.q: A digital product cost ₦72,000 to create and promote, and the seller keeps ₦4,500 per sale. How many sales to break even?
Blessing's 30-day results show 20% of approaches got replies but all paying clients came from referrals. What should her next 30 days look like?
options: Wait for clients to find her
Keep her activity target and move more approaches toward referrals, while improving her other message
finalQuiz.explain: The review is for using evidence: keep activity steady and shift effort toward the channel that converts.

capstone.title: Digital Service Launch Project
capstone.brief: Launch one clearly defined digital service (or remote job search) and document 30 days of real activity: your offer and work samples, your remote workspace and message templates, your payment and security setup, your outreach with honest results, and a 90-day plan based on what the numbers showed.
steps: Write your chosen income model and offer line, with 2 to 3 work samples (real or clearly labelled practice).
Build your remote workspace: setup sheet with data budget and backup plan, availability statement with time zone, shared Drive folder and task board.
Save your four message templates: brief confirmation, status update, delay warning and handover note.
Set up your payment route (fees checked on the official site with the date), 2-Step Verification and an income record sheet.
Make at least 40 personal approaches or 5 precise job applications over 30 days and log each one in a tracking sheet.
Review your results (reply rate, conversion, channel) and write what you learned honestly, including what did not work.
Write your 90-day plan with weekly activity targets, one improvement based on your review, and one way you will share skills or work with another woman.
evidence: Setup sheet, availability statement and screenshots of folder and task board
Payment notes, net-amount calculation and security screenshots (codes hidden)
Tracking sheet with at least 30 days of outreach or applications
Honest results review with real numbers
